storm.summary_layperson: No storms on radar and none expected tonight — a dry, mild evening, with the next chance of showers and a few thunderstorms holding off until Thursday night into Friday.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Cool Sound water (65°F) gives an 11°F protective gap at 4 PM, but it shrinks to about 4°F by 7 PM as the air cools — the buffer fades around 6:18 PM, and there's nothing for it to act on tonight anyway.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: The Upton radar shows no echoes anywhere in range and there are no NWS watches, warnings, or advisories for the area. Instability is low — about 380 J/kg of CAPE (the fuel for thunderstorms), well under the ~1500 J/kg level where storms can punch through the Sound's cool air — and the model takes it to zero after sunset. Upper-level wind shear is strong (about 54 kt from the west), but shear needs instability to work with, and tonight there isn't any.

Local effect: The Sound is 65°F and the air near shore is about 75°F, an 11°F gap. That gap matters because cool water under warmer air makes a stable layer that tends to choke storms coming off the land. It doesn't last, though: the Sound holds its temperature while the air cools after sunset, so the protective gap closes. It's projected at about 9°F at 5 PM and 6°F at 6 PM, drops below the ~5°F threshold around 6:18 PM, and is about 4°F by 7 PM.

Outcome for the cove: No storm risk tonight, here or in surrounding towns. Because there's nothing on radar to slow down or weaken, the marine layer doesn't change the forecast — we've called the local effect neutral rather than protective. Had anything been coming, it would have needed to arrive before about 6:15 PM for the Sound to help; the cool water would do little to stop anything arriving later in the evening.

Looking ahead: The NWS forecast discussion flags a strong frontal system bringing showers Thursday night into Friday morning, and a second round of showers with isolated thunderstorms late Friday afternoon and evening. The main concern there is an isolated strong wind gust; the highest severe risk is expected south of us.

What would change the call: New echoes developing to the west of the Hudson, or an NWS advisory being issued. Neither is suggested by the model or the forecasters for tonight.

wind.regime_label: Moderate westerly gradient wind — no sea breeze, fading after sunset

hourly.shift_note: right shift continuing, puffy off the land

wind.tactics_blurb: A westerly blowing down the Sound, with more pressure out toward the cove mouth than up near the shore. Lean left (south, toward open water) on the first beat while there's still breeze; if racing goes past 7 PM, protect the right because the wind will keep clocking toward the northwest.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The call: This is a moderate gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day. The air is warm enough over the land (an air–water temperature difference of about 11°F) to drive a sea breeze, but the stations aren't showing one: only about a quarter of the coastal stations have a southerly component, and the wind across the western Sound is a uniform westerly. The average wind at the well-sited airport and buoy anemometers is 9.3 kt, and Riverside YC is reading W 279° at 9.5 kt (10-minute average) with gusts to 15.

Why lean left: A westerly runs down the length of the Sound from the New York end. It's steady in direction, but it often has holes near the Connecticut shore and blows harder mid-Sound — the buoy in the western Sound shows 10.7 kt. In the cove that means more pressure toward the mouth and the open water to the south (left, looking upwind). Waterfront stations east of the cove in Old Greenwich are close to calm, which backs up the idea that the shore is the light side.

Through the window: The westerly should hold near 8 kt at 5 PM, then soften to around 6 kt as the sun goes down at 6:15 PM and the air near the surface stabilizes and cuts off the gusts. After dark it keeps easing to 4–5 kt and slowly clocks right — WNW by 8 PM and NNW to N by 9–10 PM. That's a persistent shift, not an oscillation: it keeps going one way and doesn't come back. During a 5:30–7 PM race it's only about 10°, but anyone racing later should expect the right side to pay more each leg. Northwesterly air coming off the land is puffy with holes, so by 9 PM it's drifter-class.

Model vs. stations: The HRRR forecast model has the wind at WSW (about 252°), while the stations are already at W (about 269°) — a 17° gap. On a gradient-wind day the Riverside station is the best guide to direction in the cove, so the hourly directions above are adjusted toward what the stations show. The sea-breeze direction correction doesn't apply because there's no sea breeze. The model also matches Riverside's current speed closely (8.8 vs 9.5 kt), which supports its forecast for the evening slowdown.

What the fleet will feel: At the start it's a good, raceable 8 kt with puffs in the low teens — full hiking for the lighter boats in the gusts. It gets noticeably lighter after 6 PM, and from about 7:30 PM boat speed in the light patches will matter more than sail settings. If the race committee is watching the clock, the best racing will be before sunset.

data_caveats: The latest HRRR model run (19Z) only covered up to 7 PM when we fetched it. The 8–10 PM forecast comes from the previous run (18Z, 6–8 hours out), so it's less certain.
The HRRR model doesn't give gust values. Gusts are estimated from the gust-to-average ratio at Riverside YC and are reduced after dark.
HRRR has the wind direction 17° further left than the stations (WSW 252° vs W 269°). The hourly directions are adjusted toward the stations.
Buoy 44040 (Western LIS) is out of date: wind reading 75 min old, water temperature 87 min old.
The Port Chester APRS station N1TKS is out of date (6 hours old) and excluded.
The Islip (KISP) wind sensor is down, so that station is excluded.
